Web-based veterinary management systems commonly integrate features such as appointment scheduling, electronic medical records, billing, and client communication tools into a single platform, improving workflow efficiency, reducing human error, and mitigating the risks associated with paper-based records. Leong (2023) highlights that these web-systems enable staff to manage registrations, appointments, medical records, admissions, and invoices while allowing pet owners to schedule appointments, access their pet’s medical histories, and receive timely notifications. The inclusion of automated tools, such as SMS reminders and digital report generation, further strengthens operational efficiency and client engagement.

Existing systems highlight the integration of web-based technologies to support veterinary clinic workflows and client services. According to Bucao et al. (2023), VETelgeuse, a mobile and web-based management system for small to medium-sized clinics enhance clinic-client communication, implement appointment scheduling, and support medical record management, achieving high usability and satisfaction. Blancaflor et al. (2023) report that telehealth applications for companion animal veterinarians facilitate automated appointment booking and direct integration with electronic medical records, increasing consultation capacity and supporting continuity of care. Similarly, Cachuela et al. (2025) highlight that the Veterinary Information Management System (VIMS) centralizes schedules, medical records, and client communications, improving record accuracy, reducing appointment no shows, and enhancing user satisfaction.

Despite these advances, fully integrated web-based veterinary management systems remain limited. While appointment scheduling, electronic medical records, billing, and teleconsultation technologies have developed individually, their consolidation into a unified, clinic-wide platform is still uncommon. Current solutions often rely on multiple specialized tools to address different operational needs, which can fragment workflows and reduce administrative oversight. Furthermore, systems rarely support centralized service performance reporting or real-time operational management, limiting comprehensive coordination across critical functions. These gaps highlight opportunities for a centralized platform that can unify key processes and improve clinic efficiency, data accessibility, and service quality.
Veterinary Management Systems

The growing use of digital technologies in veterinary practice has encouraged the development of management systems that can centralize clinical, administrative, and service-related information within a single platform. As veterinary clinics handle appointments, medical records, treatments, payments, inventory, and communication with pet owners, web- and mobile-based systems can provide more organized access to essential information while reducing dependence on manual and paper-based procedures. Most recently, Abd Latiff and Ab. Aziz (2025) developed EliteVet for Elite Veterinary Clinic and Surgery Tampin to address incomplete customer records and inefficient appointment processes associated with traditional operations. Using a prototyping model and an object-oriented approach, the system was developed with PHP, MySQL, and Visual Studio Code as its principal technologies and tools. It combines customer, pet, and veterinarian information with appointment scheduling, treatment documentation, pet hotel reservations, online payments, and report management. These functions reduce the inconvenience of completing printed forms and provide a centralized platform for managing clinical and administrative transactions. The study demonstrates how combining patient records, appointments, treatments, boarding services, payments, and reporting within one system can improve information accuracy, service accessibility, and the operational efficiency of veterinary clinics.

Beyond technological functions, effective veterinary management also depends on the capabilities of individuals responsible for managing clinic operations. Hompas and Liang (2025) conducted a scoping review of Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus, supplemented by a web-based review of professional institutions and postgraduate programs related to veterinary leadership and management. Fourteen articles met the inclusion criteria, revealing major concerns such as high employee attrition, stress and burnout, and insufficient investment in leadership and management development. Although more than 30 relevant skills and knowledge areas were identified, the review found limited recognition of the competencies required by veterinary managers and no coordinated framework for developing them. These findings demonstrate that effective clinic management depends not only on technological tools but also on managers who can apply evidence, manage resources and personnel, communicate effectively, lead change, and understand the veterinary environment. The authors therefore emphasized the need for a validated and comprehensive competency framework to strengthen management capability and support sustainable veterinary service delivery.

Mobile technologies have likewise been examined as tools that can support veterinary management and assist pet owners in making informed decisions regarding animal care. Haase et al. (2025) reviewed mobile health applications that can help pet owners evaluate whether their animals require professional examination while potentially reducing veterinarians’ workload. The researchers screened 955 publications and extracted ten requirements from 13 relevant sources, with the most frequently identified requirements involving complete user information and clearly displayed disclaimers regarding application limitations. Other important features included simple presentation, appropriate terminology, emergency veterinary contact details, case-specific outputs based on factors such as species, breed, age, and medical history, and documentation that veterinarians can review during consultations. The authors emphasized that user-interface design is particularly important because pet owners may have limited veterinary knowledge and animals cannot communicate their symptoms directly. These findings identify essential design and functional requirements for incorporating mobile decision support, teletriage, client communication, and clinical information collection into systems that assist veterinary professionals and support the management of animal-care services.

The need for better access to medical information across different veterinary facilities was addressed by Forja Barriga (2025) through the development of VetDataShare, a web-based platform designed to promote interoperability among veterinary centers. The system was created to address difficulties in sharing patient records, particularly during emergencies when veterinarians may require immediate access to an animal's medical information. Using the Waterfall development methodology, the application was built with Angular for the frontend, Spring Boot for the backend, and JSON Web Tokens for secure user authentication. Its primary functions include centralized medical-record management, controlled record sharing, inter-clinic collaboration, and temporary access to patient information for external veterinary professionals in specific situations. This project demonstrates how a secure and interoperable platform can improve information flow, support coordination among clinics, and provide veterinarians with timely access to clinical data for better continuity of animal care.

A comprehensive approach to managing both clinical and administrative activities was also presented by Ortiz Hernández and Guale Vera (2025), who developed a web-based veterinary management system for Agroveterinaria “La Finca.” The system was designed to address problems caused by manually recording medical information, inventory, and daily sales. Its functions include managing agricultural and veterinary product inventories, tracking expiration dates, processing sales and invoices, registering suppliers, maintaining pet and medical records, scheduling appointments, administering users, analyzing sales, and sending reminders. Surveys, interviews, and system testing showed that the modules successfully performed their intended functions and were feasible for users. These findings suggest that a web-based platform can organize clinical and administrative information, reduce dependence on manual records, and support more efficient veterinary service operations.

Earlier developments in 2023 also demonstrated the importance of centralized digital systems for managing different aspects of veterinary clinic operations. Jamil et al. (2023) developed a web-based veterinary clinic management system to address the inefficiencies and risks associated with manually recording pet, owner, appointment, and payment information. The system was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, and SQL-based database tools and provides administrators with modules for managing pets, pet owners, veterinarians, appointments, and payments. Its dashboard displays key operational information, including the number of pets and appointments and the clinic’s total revenue, while stored records can be retrieved and updated when necessary. The system also supports medical-history storage, inventory tracking, financial record management, and customized reporting. This project demonstrates how centralized digital records can reduce paperwork and data-loss risks, provide faster access to clinical and financial information, lower administrative costs, and support more organized veterinary operations. However, the researchers also identified implementation cost, data security, and staff adoption as important considerations for successful deployment.

The convenience of managing veterinary appointments and related information online was further examined by Mohd Yusof and Mohd Fauzi (2023). Their web-based veterinary clinic management system was designed to replace manual appointment procedures and provide pet owners with a more convenient way to request veterinary services. The system allows users to manage appointment-related information, including schedules, assessments, self-reports, and notifications, before visiting the clinic. Findings indicated that users could operate and manage the system effectively and that it fulfilled their intended appointment-management needs. These results demonstrate how online scheduling, preliminary pet-health reporting, assessment management, and automated notifications can work together within a single platform to improve appointment administration, user convenience, and the delivery of veterinary care.
Online Consultation in Veterinary Clinics

The development of online consultation in veterinary medicine has continued to expand as digital technologies provide new ways for veterinarians to communicate with pet owners and deliver remote services. In a recent mixed-methods study, Karsch et al. (2026) examined the perspectives of 404 pet owners and veterinary experts and found strong demand for flexible digital consultation services in small-animal practice. The study demonstrated that teleconsultations can provide time savings, reduce animal stress, and improve service convenience. Nevertheless, technical barriers and the inability to perform physical examinations were identified as important limitations. These findings reinforce the importance of developing hybrid veterinary service models in which online consultation complements rather than completely replaces face-to-face veterinary care.

Looking at veterinary telehealth across different practice settings, Neill et al. (2025) investigated its use among veterinarians in rural and urban areas. The study found comparable adoption patterns between the two geographic groups and noted that online consultations can help address workforce shortages while extending the reach of veterinary services. This suggests that telemedicine can serve as a practical means of expanding veterinary care regardless of location, particularly in areas where access to veterinary professionals or specialized services is limited.

Veterinary telemedicine has also gained attention as a digital approach for improving access to animal healthcare. According to Abu-Seida (2024), veterinary telemedicine enables electronic communication for remote consultation, diagnosis, and treatment, thereby expanding access to veterinary services. The author explained that the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated its adoption because of mobility restrictions and the growing demand for remote services. However, regulatory concerns, particularly the requirement for a valid Veterinary-Client-Patient Relationship (VCPR), remain important considerations. Despite these limitations, telemedicine provides veterinary clinics with opportunities to extend their services and improve communication with pet owners.
Inventory Management in Veterinary Clinics

The management of veterinary medicines, vaccines, medical supplies, and other clinic products has become an important part of maintaining continuous animal healthcare and efficient veterinary operations. As veterinary clinics handle different inventory items with varying levels of demand, cost, criticality, and storage requirements, effective inventory practices are necessary to prevent shortages, excess stock, expiration, and other forms of wastage. The growing use of computerized systems and analytical inventory-control methods has also provided veterinary practices with opportunities to monitor stock levels, determine replenishment requirements, and use inventory data to support operational decisions. Most recently, Ayalew et al. (2026) developed an inventory-management framework that combines ABC analysis, VED classification, and multi-criteria analysis to support pharmaceutical inventory decisions. The framework considered factors such as consumption value, criticality, and other inventory-related characteristics to classify medicines more comprehensively. It also incorporated demand forecasting, Economic Order Quantity, reorder points, and safety stock to support inventory-level and replenishment decisions. Although conducted in a human healthcare setting, the study demonstrates how analytical approaches can assist organizations in prioritizing medicines, allocating resources, determining replenishment requirements, and controlling inventory costs. These principles can likewise support the systematic management of medicines and supplies in veterinary clinics.

A broader computerized approach was also presented by Ranido et al. (2026), who developed a web- and mobile-based Veterinary Clinic Management System for the Balingasag Veterinary Clinic. The proposed system incorporated electronic health records, appointment scheduling, inventory management, telemedicine, SMS notifications, pet monitoring, and other clinic functions. The study used a developmental research design and an Agile development approach, while the proposed system was evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model. Although inventory management is only one component of the system, the study provides supporting evidence for incorporating computerized inventory functions into veterinary clinic operations alongside clinical, administrative, and communication services.

In 2025, several studies further examined the role of data-driven systems and systematic inventory practices in addressing common veterinary inventory concerns. Bustamante-León et al. (2025) developed specialized software for a veterinary clinic in Guayaquil to address stock mismanagement, excess unsold products, shortages of high-demand items, and human errors. The methodology included interviews with inventory managers, historical data analysis, and root-cause analysis tools such as the Ishikawa Diagram, Pareto Analysis, and the 5 Whys. The proposed software incorporated the Economic Order Quantity and Silver-Meal models to determine optimal inventory quantities and reorder points while accounting for changes in demand. Results demonstrated reductions in inventory errors, excess stock, and shortages, together with improvements in operational efficiency. These findings demonstrate how data-driven software can support inventory decisions, improve stock control, and address common inventory-related problems in veterinary practices.

The prevention of pharmaceutical expiration was another important concern examined by Mekasha et al. (2025). Their mixed-methods study involved animal health facilities in South Wollo, Ethiopia, and assessed the magnitude, economic impact, and factors associated with expired veterinary pharmaceuticals. The researchers identified inadequate inventory control, store-management problems, and weaknesses in pharmaceutical management policies and guidelines as factors associated with pharmaceutical expiration. The findings emphasize the importance of appropriate inventory control and store-management practices in reducing pharmaceutical expiration and its associated financial impact. Thus, effective veterinary inventory management is important not only for maintaining stock availability but also for reducing losses associated with expired products.

A technology-based approach to pharmaceutical monitoring was presented by Rathod and Patil (2025) through the development of MediVax, a desktop-based pharmaceutical inventory management system intended for veterinary and healthcare industries. Developed using Java and MySQL, the system incorporates inventory tracking, procurement management, sales processing, report generation, secure user identification, and real-time vaccine temperature monitoring. It also includes alerts for temperature irregularities and inventory shortages. The system was designed to support regulatory compliance, reduce waste, and improve operational efficiency in pharmaceutical management. This study demonstrates how a digital inventory system can combine stock monitoring with environmental monitoring for temperature-sensitive veterinary pharmaceutical products.

The application of centralized systems can likewise support inventory management within veterinary clinics. Diego et al. (2025) developed a web-based Veterinary Clinic Management System for FurCare Veterinary Clinic to address problems associated with manual record-keeping and disconnected systems. The system includes online appointment scheduling, automated SMS reminders, digital medical records, and real-time inventory tracking. Evaluation reported improvements in speed, accuracy, and user satisfaction, with a System Usability Scale score of 86.5. These findings demonstrate that real-time inventory tracking can be incorporated into a centralized veterinary management system to improve access to inventory information and support more organized clinic operations.

A similar approach was demonstrated by Cabactulan et al. (2025), who developed a Multi-Branch Veterinary Clinic Management System to improve efficiency, accuracy, and coordination across multiple clinic branches. The system includes centralized record management, appointment scheduling, inventory monitoring, billing, inter-branch referrals, and SMS notifications. Functional testing achieved a 100% pass rate, while usability evaluation using the System Usability Scale produced a score of 70.8. The study shows that centralized veterinary management systems can support inventory monitoring and provide access to inventory information across clinic branches, making computerized systems useful for managing veterinary clinic inventory.

The availability, storage, and handling of veterinary drugs were also examined by Mekonen et al. (2025) as important factors in maintaining medicine quality and supporting effective animal healthcare services. The researchers conducted a cross-sectional study involving government veterinary clinics and private veterinary pharmacies in and around Nekemte Town, Ethiopia. The study assessed veterinary drug availability, storage conditions, and the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of veterinary professionals concerning veterinary medicine management. Challenges involving drug availability, storage conditions, and the safe management of veterinary pharmaceuticals were identified.

From the perspective of inventory prioritization, Sinha and Singh (2025) evaluated pharmaceutical inventory management in a tertiary care teaching hospital using ABC, VED, and integrated ABC-VED analysis. The study identified high-cost medicines requiring closer monitoring and demonstrated how these methods can assist in prioritizing pharmaceutical inventory. It also identified operational challenges involving inventory management and emphasized the importance of regular inventory evaluation and improved control procedures. Although the study was conducted in a human hospital, its systematic approach to pharmaceutical classification and prioritization is relevant to veterinary clinics that manage medicines and other pharmaceutical supplies.

Drug-storage practices among veterinary professionals were also examined by Perry and Gouveia (2025) in the United Kingdom. Using a questionnaire-based approach, the researchers focused on the conditions and procedures involved in storing veterinary medicines. The study identified factors that may increase risks associated with inappropriate storage and emphasized the importance of proper storage practices and management procedures for maintaining veterinary medicine quality. Although its primary focus is drug storage rather than inventory management as a whole, the findings remain relevant because storage is an important component of maintaining pharmaceutical inventory quality and preventing losses caused by improper handling or storage.

The importance of understanding pharmaceutical consumption was further demonstrated by Romero et al. (2025), who conducted a retrospective study at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of the University of León in Spain. The researchers examined perioperative drug use among companion animals from 2018 to 2022 and analyzed prescription patterns and variables associated with medication use during surgical care. The study identified commonly used medication categories and emphasized that examining drug-utilization patterns can support evidence-based decisions and promote appropriate pharmaceutical use. Although the research focused primarily on medication utilization rather than inventory control, its analysis of pharmaceutical consumption provides useful information for understanding medicine-use patterns that influences inventory planning in veterinary settings.

As inventory systems and analytical approaches continued to develop, research in 2024 examined different methods for improving stock control and pharmaceutical management. Mekonen et al. (2024) investigated veterinary pharmaceutical warehouse-management practices and emphasized their importance in maintaining the quality and availability of veterinary pharmaceuticals and supporting animal health services. The researchers assessed warehouse-management practices and associated challenges in selected areas of Ethiopia, including veterinary pharmaceutical management in government veterinary clinics and private veterinary drug wholesalers. The study identified weaknesses in warehouse-management practices and other supply-chain activities that can affect the quality and availability of veterinary supplies. These findings emphasize the importance of appropriate procedures for receiving, storing, and issuing veterinary pharmaceuticals, as systematic control over pharmaceutical stocks and their storage conditions is essential to reliable inventory operations.
Online Appointment Scheduling in Veterinary Clinics

The shift from manual to digital veterinary services has encouraged the development of online systems that provide pet owners with easier access to clinic schedules, veterinarian availability, and appointment booking. As veterinary clinics continue to adopt web-based technologies, digital scheduling platforms have become increasingly important in allowing clients to arrange veterinary services conveniently while helping clinic personnel manage appointments more effectively. Most recently, Decolongon et al. (2026) developed an integrated web-based system that combines veterinary appointment scheduling, pet product shopping, and online payment services. Its appointment module enables clients to schedule veterinary services online, select specific services, and view the availability of veterinarians, reducing delays and unnecessary back-and-forth communication between clients and clinic personnel. Developed using an Agile approach, the system was evaluated through user acceptability testing and the ISO/IEC 25010:2011 software quality model. The veterinary appointment scheduling feature received a mean score of 4.0, interpreted as Strongly Agree, while the ability to display veterinarian availability also received a score of 4.0. Overall user acceptability reached a grand mean of 3.9, interpreted as Very Good. These findings demonstrate that digital appointment booking, service selection, and veterinarian availability can make scheduling more accessible and convenient while reducing administrative tasks for veterinary clinics.

Similarly, Ranido et al. (2026) proposed a web- and mobile-based Veterinary Clinic Management System for the Balingasag Dog and Cat Pet’s Clinic in Misamis Oriental in response to operational inefficiencies associated with manual appointment scheduling and paper-based records. The proposed system includes automated appointment scheduling, electronic health records, SMS notifications, real-time telemedicine, inventory management, pet monitoring, announcements, and client feedback functions within a single platform. The study employed a developmental research design using the Agile development approach, while the proposed system was evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model with veterinary staff and pet owners as respondents. By addressing limitations associated with manual processes, the system demonstrates the continued movement toward digital platforms that can improve veterinary operations, appointment management, and communication between clinics and pet owners.

As online veterinary services progressed into 2025, researchers continued to examine the usability and effectiveness of dedicated appointment booking platforms. Rosmani and Mokhtar (2025) designed and developed an online appointment booking system to simplify the scheduling process for veterinary clinic users. Using the waterfall development model, the system was developed through requirement analysis, design, coding, testing, and implementation. Functionality and usability testing showed that the majority of users considered the system simple to use. The researchers concluded that the online scheduling platform made the appointment process easier, demonstrating the potential of web-based booking systems to improve accessibility and usability for veterinary clinic clients.

Addressing common problems associated with manual appointment processes, Cachuela et al. (2025) developed a web-based Veterinary Information Management System that allows pet owners to access appointment availability without physically visiting the clinic. The system was designed to address appointment overlaps, scheduling conflicts, and wasted time. It was evaluated using ISO/IEC 25010 standards for functionality, performance, and usability, while user satisfaction was assessed through the Technology Acceptance Model. Results from 50 participants showed an excellent technical quality rating of 4.63 out of 5.00 and a very good user satisfaction rating of 3.68 out of 5.00. Following implementation, the clinic also experienced a 40% reduction in appointment no-shows. These findings suggest that providing online access to appointment availability can improve the management of clinic schedules while contributing to better attendance among clients.

The effects of online appointment scheduling on appointment utilization were further examined outside the veterinary field by Kammrath Betancor et al. (2025). Their retrospective two-center observational study analyzed 16,894 appointments in an ophthalmology practice and 81,173 appointments in a university hospital over a 20-month period. In the private practice, online-booked appointments had a significantly lower no-show rate than offline bookings, at 1.8% compared with 5.9%. After the implementation of online appointment scheduling, unused appointments decreased from 22.7% to 10.3%, while never-booked appointment slots declined from 8.6% to 1.6%. However, the university hospital showed a different pattern, with online-scheduled appointments having a higher no-show rate than offline appointments, indicating that the effectiveness of online scheduling may vary according to the healthcare setting. SMS reminders were also found to help reduce the risk of missed appointments. These findings are relevant to veterinary clinics because similar systems can provide pet owners with flexible digital booking, cancellation, and rescheduling options while helping clinics make better use of available appointment slots.

A more comprehensive approach to veterinary clinic management was presented by Diego et al. (2025) through a centralized web-based system developed for FurCare Veterinary Clinic. The system includes online appointment scheduling, automated SMS reminders, digital medical records, and real-time inventory tracking for administrators, veterinarians, staff, and pet owners. Its scheduling function prevents double-booking by making reserved time slots unavailable to other pet owners, while automated reminders support timely communication regarding scheduled visits. Using an Agile development approach, the system was evaluated based on functionality, performance, and usability, with results showing improvements in operational speed, accuracy, and user satisfaction. The system achieved an overall usability score of 86.5, demonstrating how centralized booking, automated reminders, and controlled appointment availability can reduce scheduling conflicts and improve the efficiency and reliability of veterinary appointment management.

In 2024, online appointment scheduling systems increasingly focused on giving pet owners greater control over the booking process. Kamle (2024) explained that an online appointment booking system can make veterinary services more convenient and efficient by allowing pet owners to schedule appointments without relying on phone calls or in-person visits. The proposed system allows users to check veterinarian availability, select a specific veterinarian based on specialization, choose an available appointment slot, and provide information about the animal’s condition and symptoms through an online form. The study also emphasized the importance of convenience and clear communication between pet owners and veterinary clinics throughout the booking process.

Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) have become increasingly important in veterinary medicine because they provide a centralized and accessible means of managing patient information, supporting clinical decision-making, improving communication, and strengthening the delivery of veterinary services. Recent developments have also demonstrated that electronic records can extend beyond basic documentation by supporting secure information sharing, research, patient safety, and data-driven clinical practices.

The importance of secure and accessible veterinary records was demonstrated by Mattur et al. (2026), who developed a web-based Electronic Health Record Management System for pet care and adoption. The system centralized pet medical information, vaccination records, checkup schedules, and adoption-related information in a single platform. To protect sensitive information, the researchers implemented role-based access control, password hashing, token-based authentication, and audit logging, ensuring that only authorized users could access specific records. The system also supported reliable record management and efficient synchronization of updates among veterinarians, pet owners, and adopters. These findings demonstrate that security and controlled access are essential components of veterinary EMR systems, particularly when patient information must be shared among multiple stakeholders.

Beyond veterinary practice, Jones et al. (2026) found that implementing an EMR system in an outpatient healthcare clinic significantly improved time efficiency, data accuracy, cost savings, and healthcare worker satisfaction. However, the study also identified challenges involving limited computer equipment, network interruptions, unstable electricity, and differences in users’ technological skills. The researchers emphasized that adequate infrastructure and regular training are necessary to maximize the benefits of electronic records. These findings are applicable to veterinary clinics because successful EMR adoption likewise depends on reliable equipment, stable connectivity, and sufficient staff competency.

Further developments in veterinary EMR systems were reported by Davies et al. (2025), who discussed the use of veterinary electronic health records as real-world data sources for pharmacoepidemiological research. The authors demonstrated that semi-structured treatment data combined with free-text clinical narratives can support cohort analysis and risk estimation in veterinary populations. They also emphasized that EHR systems can expand pharmacovigilance capabilities when supported by appropriate text-mining and data-standardization techniques.

In a related application, Petrou et al. (2025) examined first-opinion veterinary practice EHRs to identify medication errors in clinical settings. The researchers found that electronic records can reveal dosing errors and other treatment-related risks that may remain underreported through voluntary reporting systems. Their findings demonstrate the contribution of EMR infrastructures to patient safety, clinical governance, and medication management. Properly maintained electronic records can therefore help veterinary professionals identify recurring errors and improve clinical procedures.

The analytical potential of structured veterinary EMR data was further demonstrated by Farrell et al. (2025), who introduced PetEVAL, a benchmark dataset containing 17,600 real-world veterinary electronic health records annotated for disease and syndromic analysis. Their work showed that large and well-structured EMR datasets can support the development of natural language processing and other analytical tools for veterinary medicine. The researchers emphasized that greater access to standardized digital records can encourage innovation in animal health monitoring and comparative biomedical research. This demonstrates that properly structured EMRs can support emerging technologies for analyzing and interpreting animal health information.

Security and reliable information sharing have also become important considerations in veterinary EMR development. Khafagy et al. (2025) developed VetChain-RAG, a blockchain-enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework designed to securely retrieve, verify, and analyze veterinary case records. Blockchain technology was used to support the authenticity and integrity of electronic medical records while enabling privacy-preserving data sharing among veterinary institutions. Experimental validation demonstrated reliable retrieval of historical patient records and secure access to clinical information. The researchers concluded that combining blockchain with AI-powered retrieval systems can strengthen the security, accessibility, and reliability of veterinary EMRs while supporting more informed clinical decision-making.

The effectiveness of EMRs in improving documentation was also examined by Torab-Miandoab et al. (2025), who developed and implemented an EMR system in the VIP department of Shahid Madani Hospital at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences. The researchers compared 351 electronic and paper-based patient files using criteria such as comprehensiveness, relevance, precision, accuracy, readability, consistency, and completeness. The findings showed that the EMR system reduced the average documentation time from 120 minutes to 45 minutes and improved the evaluated documentation standards to 100%. The researchers also emphasized that customizing EMR systems according to user needs and providing appropriate training can further improve documentation practices and user satisfaction. These suggest that veterinary EMRs can similarly reduce documentation time while improving the accuracy, completeness, and organization of animal patient records.

Likewise, Cahyaningrum et al. (2025) developed a web-based EMR information system to address problems associated with paper-based records, including delayed access to patient information, duplicate records, and document loss. The system enabled faster retrieval of patient information, reduced duplication, and improved documentation accuracy. During testing, the system contributed to a 35% increase in service efficiency. The researchers recommended further development through cloud-based and mobile applications. These findings reinforce the value of centralized digital records in veterinary clinics, where fast and accurate access to animal patient information is necessary for efficient service delivery.

In another healthcare setting, Farrant et al. (2025) examined the implementation of a clinically based EMR system in a Division I athletic medicine clinic. The system improved documentation quality, communication, and operational efficiency by allowing healthcare professionals to standardize clinical documentation, manage billing processes, and share patient information across the medical system. However, the researchers noted that staff training, organizational support, and adjustments to traditional documentation practices were necessary for successful implementation. This suggests that veterinary clinics can also benefit from standardized EMR systems while recognizing the importance of staff readiness and organizational support.

Within veterinary practice specifically, Cachuela et al. (2025) developed a Web-Based Veterinary Information Management System for Animals’ Choice Clinic to address difficulties associated with manual appointment scheduling and paper-based medical records. Using Agile Scrum methodology, the researchers developed a system that digitalized pet medical records, improved appointment management, and strengthened communication between veterinary staff and pet owners. The system obtained an excellent technical quality rating, with a mean score of 4.63 out of 5.00, while user satisfaction received a very good mean score of 3.68 out of 5.00. The implementation also contributed to a 40% reduction in appointment no-shows and improved the accuracy of pet medical records.

Moving to developments in 2024, Kanavin and Agoltsov (2024) found that electronic patient records, electronic document management systems, clinic automation software, and other digital technologies can improve administrative and clinical processes in both private and public veterinary sectors. Their findings showed that digital record management provides faster access to patient information, improves communication with clients, reduces administrative workload, strengthens animal health monitoring, and contributes to better-quality veterinary services.
Queue Management in Veterinary Clinics

Effective queue management is an important aspect of veterinary clinic operations because the number of clients and animals seeking services may vary throughout the day, while the availability of veterinarians, consultation rooms, and other resources may be limited. Recent developments in healthcare information systems have shown that digital queue monitoring, appointment scheduling, virtual ticketing, and data-driven approaches can improve patient flow and reduce waiting times. These approaches are applicable to veterinary clinics because similar challenges may occur during registration, consultation, vaccination, treatment, and other services.Recently, Kandekar et al. (2026) introduced the Clinic Queue Handler Web Portal, a web-based queue management system designed to improve patient flow and reduce waiting times. The system incorporated real-time queue tracking, automated token generation, appointment scheduling, role-based access control, and a Patient Treatment Time Prediction (PTTP) algorithm. It also included a Hospital Queuing-Recommendation (HQR) module that recommended treatment schedules according to estimated service requirements. Additional functions included SMS and email notifications, doctor dashboards, and connections with Electronic Health Records and billing systems. The implementation reduced manual record-keeping and improved transparency between healthcare providers and patients. Similar functions can be applied to veterinary clinics to manage appointments, monitor waiting times, estimate service duration, and coordinate veterinary personnel.

Similarly, Fauzi and Suhaimi (2026) developed QKlinik, a web-based queue management system intended to improve patient flow in outpatient clinics. Using Agile Scrum methodology, the researchers incorporated online queue registration, real-time queue monitoring, appointment scheduling, automated notifications, and a user-friendly interface for patients and healthcare providers. Evaluation of the system demonstrated improvements in queue organization, communication, and user satisfaction. These features can be adapted to veterinary clinics by allowing pet owners to register online, monitor their queue position, receive appointment reminders, and obtain notifications when their consultation is approaching. Such a platform can reduce unnecessary waiting and improve the organization of veterinary services.

Another recent development was presented by Jadhav et al. (2026), who developed MediQueue, a machine-learning-based healthcare queue optimization framework addressing overcrowding, prolonged waiting times, inefficient scheduling, and uneven resource utilization. The system incorporated predictive analytics, real-time patient information, intelligent scheduling, and cloud-based healthcare management. Appointment records, provider availability, treatment duration, and emergency priorities were considered when classifying patients and dynamically adjusting queue strategies. Historical and real-time data were also used to predict congestion and optimize appointment allocation. These methods can be applied to veterinary clinics because client volume, consultation duration, veterinarian availability, and the urgency of animal cases may vary considerably. A similar approach could help predict high-demand periods, prioritize cases, manage appointments, and allocate veterinary resources more effectively.

Within the veterinary setting, Kirana (2025) discussed the development of a web-based medical record and veterinary clinic service information system at the UPTD Veterinary Health Clinic in Medan City. Service Performance Reporting System

The growing reliance on digital technologies has increased the importance of structured reporting systems that can transform operational data into measurable information for evaluating service outcomes and supporting management decisions. Performance reporting serves as an important mechanism for monitoring organizational activities, assessing results, identifying areas that require attention, and promoting accountability. As organizations continue to generate larger amounts of service-related data, digital reporting tools can provide timely and organized information on operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, employee performance, and other measurable indicators. Most recently, Ranido et al. (2026) proposed a web- and mobile-based Veterinary Clinic Management System for the Balingasag Dog and Cat Pet’s Clinic in response to inefficiencies associated with paper-based records, manual appointment scheduling, and limited communication systems. The proposed system enables pet owners to record symptoms and behavioral changes and generate health summary reports for veterinarian review. Its digital records, feedback, monitoring, and report-generation functions provide structured information that can be used to assess veterinary service activities and operational performance. By consolidating service-related information within a digital platform, clinic management can monitor service delivery, identify operational concerns, evaluate outcomes, and use generated reports as a basis for informed decision-making and continuous improvement.

A related approach was presented by Decolongon et al. (2026), who developed a web-based system that combines veterinary appointment scheduling, pet product shopping, online payments, veterinarian availability, and monthly sales analytics. The system was evaluated through Alpha and Beta testing using performance measures such as effectiveness, efficiency, user satisfaction, risk reduction, and context coverage. It achieved a grand mean of 3.9 for user acceptability, while its software quality based on ISO/IEC 25010 received a grand mean of 3.5, indicating generally favorable performance and acceptance. Notably, the platform included an analytics feature for tracking total monthly sales, demonstrating how operational data can be transformed into measurable information for monitoring organizational activities. These findings show how a veterinary clinic can use a digital platform to organize operational records, track performance indicators and trends, evaluate efficiency and user satisfaction, and provide structured information for assessing service performance.

The importance of clearly defined expectations and regular evaluation was further emphasized by Sasmita et al. (2026) in relation to veterinary personnel performance. The study found that effective performance appraisal, continuous improvement, and talent management are important factors in improving employee productivity and performance. Performance appraisal was found to improve productivity by establishing clear expectations, providing developmental feedback, and strengthening employee accountability. The authors also reported that applying these management practices together produced greater productivity benefits within the context of veterinary clinics. These findings demonstrate the importance of clearly defined performance measures, regular evaluation, and accountability. A reporting system can record and present employee and service performance indicators, allowing management to compare results with established expectations, identify performance gaps, provide appropriate feedback, monitor improvements over time, and support decisions aimed at improving staff productivity and veterinary service quality.

Digital performance management was also examined by Anam and Nyong (2026), who described performance management systems as important mechanisms for improving service efficiency, accountability, employee productivity, and service delivery. Using a qualitative and doctrinal approach, the researchers synthesized existing literature, policy reports, and comparative public administration studies. Their findings showed that performance appraisal, results-based management, performance contracting, and digital performance tracking can contribute to greater organizational efficiency and responsiveness. The study further emphasized that automated monitoring systems and electronic reporting frameworks enable real-time performance tracking and can reduce administrative inefficiencies. These findings support the development of a Service Performance Reporting System that can monitor outputs, evaluate results, provide feedback, and present timely information for continuous improvement and management decision-making.

These findings demonstrate how measurable operational indicators and automated reports can be used to evaluate service efficiency, monitor improvements over time, and provide management with concrete information for assessing operational performance.

In 2025, research continued to demonstrate the value of structured performance reporting in supporting organizational evaluation and decision-making. Israwati et al. These findings demonstrate how a technology-supported reporting system can facilitate the collection, organization, monitoring, and documentation of performance data while reducing delays and inconsistencies associated with manual reporting.

The findings emphasized the importance of a transparent and responsive system for tracking measurable outcomes while keeping daily activities aligned with long-term objectives. These findings demonstrate the importance of a reporting system that can organize relevant indicators, compare actual performance with established standards, identify performance gaps, and provide reliable reports that support monitoring, evaluation, accountability, and evidence-based improvements in veterinary service delivery.

Digital technologies enable organizations to use performance information more dynamically for monitoring progress, focusing attention on organizational priorities, supporting strategic decision-making, and maintaining accountability. For veterinary clinics, a highly usable POS system can simplify billing, medicine and vaccine inventory monitoring, appointment-related transactions, and sales of veterinary products. The findings showed that the platform improved appointment scheduling, simplified online purchasing, increased transaction accuracy, and reduced administrative workload. Although the system extended beyond traditional POS functions, its integration of e-commerce and payment capabilities demonstrates how POS-related technologies can be incorporated into broader veterinary information systems. Such an approach can allow veterinary clinics to manage product sales, appointments, payments, and client interactions through a unified platform while improving accessibility and customer convenience.

The researchers will use the Incremental Development Model for the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The researcher will use the model to allow developing the system by dividing the requirements in parts of functional modules called increments, where each increment adds new features and improvements to the system until the final product is completed. The proposed system incremental will first undergo requirement analysis, followed by design and development, testing, and deployment of each module. Figure 3 illustrates the Incremental Development Model used in the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The Incremental Model is a software development approach that focuses on building the system gradually through a series of smaller development cycles called increments. Each increment follows a structured process consisting of requirement analysis, system design, development, testing, and deployment, allowing a portion of the system to be completed and evaluated before moving on to the next stage. In this model, the core functionalities of the system are developed first, followed by additional features that enhance the system in later increments. Each increment produces a functional component of the system that can be tested and improved before integrating it into the overall platform. This process ensures that errors are identified early and that system improvements can be implemented continuously throughout development.

Every increment will have a minimum duration of one month and a maximum duration of one month and two weeks, depending on the complexity of the features being implemented. During this period, the researchers will conduct requirement adjustment, system design, module development, and testing activities before proceeding to the succeeding increment. This time-bounded approach ensures that each module is properly developed and evaluated while maintaining steady progress in the overall system development.

Each increment will focus on implementing specific modules and system functionalities, allowing the researchers to progressively build, evaluate, and refine the system until the complete platform is achieved.

Results indicated that appropriate distribution of tasks improved clinic productivity while reducing the workload of veterinarians, which ultimately contributed to the financial sustainability of veterinary practices. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating operational strategies to ensure efficient use of resources in veterinary clinics. In the context of the present study, veterinary clinic systems can help track staff responsibilities, service activities, and operational expenditures, thereby providing valuable information for conducting cost-benefit analysis.
Synthesis

The reviewed literature demonstrates the increasing use of digital technologies in veterinary healthcare to improve clinic operations, service accessibility, and information management. Across the different studies, researchers consistently describe the movement from manual administrative processes toward computerized systems that support veterinary services, client interaction, and clinic management functions. These developments illustrate how digital systems contribute to more organized veterinary operations and improved service delivery.

Research on veterinary management systems shows that early system implementations were developed to address challenges associated with paper-based records and manual appointment scheduling. According to Jaffar and Zin (2021), web-based veterinary platforms were initially introduced to facilitate online registration, appointment scheduling, and access to treatment information, thereby improving service coordination. Later studies expanded these capabilities by enabling secure storage of medical histories, appointment monitoring, and generation of administrative reports that support clinic management (Jamil, 2023; Ahmad & Salamat, 2023). More recent research demonstrates that veterinary management systems now include additional modules such as inventory tracking, financial management, and centralized record sharing among clinics (Abd Latiff & Aziz, 2025; Guale Vera, 2025; Silva & Reis, 2025). These developments indicate that modern veterinary information systems increasingly support comprehensive operational management within clinical environments.

Studies examining online appointment scheduling in veterinary clinics show that digital booking systems improve accessibility and organization of veterinary services. Researchers report that web-based scheduling platforms reduce reliance on phone-based booking and allow pet owners to arrange consultations more conveniently (Blancaflor et al., 2023; Bucao et al., 2023). In addition, several investigations demonstrate that online scheduling contributes to reduced administrative workload and fewer booking errors (Rosmani & Mokhtar, 2023). Empirical findings further indicate measurable improvements in clinic operations, including decreased appointment no-show rates, increased appointment utilization, and improved after-hours booking accessibility (Cachuela et al., 2025; Larkin, 2023; MWI Animal Health, 2024). These results show that online scheduling systems play a significant role in improving veterinary service accessibility and appointment management.

The literature also discusses the growing use of online consultation and telemedicine in veterinary practice. Studies show that telehealth platforms improve access to veterinary care, particularly for clients who experience transportation or financial limitations (Lundahl et al., 2022; Naimark et al., 2022). Remote consultations allow veterinarians to provide guidance, follow-up care, and preliminary assessments without requiring immediate physical visits, which may reduce stress for animals and increase convenience for pet owners (Addae, 2023; Guintard et al., 2024). Despite these advantages, researchers note that adoption may be influenced by factors such as technological familiarity, regulatory policies, and concerns regarding diagnostic limitations in remote consultations (Abu-Seida, 2024; Springer, 2024). Nevertheless, recent studies indicate growing interest in hybrid care approaches that combine digital consultation with traditional in-clinic examinations (Neill, 2025; Karsch, 2026).

Another important component discussed in the literature is the implementation of electronic medical record (EMR) systems in veterinary clinics. These systems support efficient documentation, retrieval, and sharing of animal health information. According to Ouyang (2021), modern veterinary practice increasingly requires digital tools that allow effective communication and information exchange between veterinarians and pet owners. Subsequent studies confirm that EMR systems improve clinical documentation processes and facilitate continuity of care by allowing veterinarians to access patient histories more easily (Ahmed et al., 2023). Furthermore, electronic records provide valuable resources for broader veterinary research, disease surveillance, and medication monitoring when large numbers of records are examined collectively (Fins et al., 2023; Davies et al., 2024). Client portals connected to these systems also enable pet owners to review vaccination records, treatment histories, and appointment information, strengthening transparency and client participation in animal healthcare (Aristek Systems, 2025).

The reviewed studies also emphasize the importance of queue management systems in improving service flow within healthcare environments, including veterinary clinics. Research indicates that digital queue systems allow clinics to monitor waiting lines, organize service order, and reduce waiting time (Bidari et al., 2021; Ala et al., 2022). Implementations of electronic queue platforms have been shown to reduce congestion in reception areas and improve patient flow within clinical facilities (Okunade et al., 2024; Rachmawati et al., 2024). Additional investigations demonstrate that advanced queue optimization techniques, including predictive modeling and automated monitoring tools, can further improve service responsiveness and reduce waiting stress among clients (Tshiamala et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest that digital queue management contributes to more organized and efficient service processes in veterinary clinics.

In addition, several studies discuss the role of service performance reporting systems in supporting organizational monitoring and evaluation. Digital reporting frameworks allow institutions to record operational indicators and generate reports that support management decision-making (Tiron-Tudor et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024). Automated reporting tools also help reduce errors associated with manual documentation while improving transparency and accountability in service operations (Santos et al., 2024; OECD, 2025). Through structured performance monitoring, institutions can better assess service quality, identify operational issues, and support continuous improvement efforts.

Finally, the literature emphasizes the relevance of the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model in evaluating veterinary information systems. Studies show that this framework provides a structured approach for assessing software quality characteristics such as functionality, usability, reliability, security, performance efficiency, maintainability, and compatibility (Iskandar et al., 2023; Matias et al., 2025). Research further indicates that veterinary systems must ensure secure handling of clinical information, dependable system operation, and user-friendly interfaces to support effective veterinary service delivery (Bök et al., 2024; Ganiron et al., 2026). Applying ISO25010 therefore provides a comprehensive basis for evaluating the quality and effectiveness of veterinary clinic information systems.

Overall, the reviewed literature indicates that digital veterinary systems play a significant role in improving clinic management, service accessibility, and veterinary healthcare delivery. The studies collectively show that technologies such as online appointment scheduling, teleconsultation platforms, electronic medical records, queue management systems, and performance reporting tools help address limitations associated with manual clinic processes. At the same time, the literature suggests that successful system implementation depends on usability, technical infrastructure, and regulatory considerations. These insights provide a strong foundation for developing veterinary information systems that effectively support both clinic operations and client engagement.
Software Methodology

The researchers will use the Incremental Development Model for the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The researcher will use the model to allow developing the system by dividing the requirements in parts of functional modules called increments, where each increment adds new features and improvements to the system until the final product is completed. The proposed system incremental will first undergo requirement analysis, followed by design and development, testing, and deployment of each module. Each increment will produce a working portion of the system that will be evaluated and refined before proceeding to the next stage of development.

Figure 3 illustrates the Incremental Development Model used in the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The Incremental Model is a software development approach that focuses on building the system gradually through a series of smaller development cycles called increments. Each increment follows a structured process consisting of requirement analysis, system design, development, testing, and deployment, allowing a portion of the system to be completed and evaluated before moving on to the next stage. In this model, the core functionalities of the system are developed first, followed by additional features that enhance the system in later increments. Each increment produces a functional component of the system that can be tested and improved before integrating it into the overall platform. This process ensures that errors are identified early and that system improvements can be implemented continuously throughout development.

Every increment will have a minimum duration of one month and a maximum duration of one month and two weeks, depending on the complexity of the features being implemented. During this period, the researchers will conduct requirement adjustment, system design, module development, and testing activities before proceeding to the succeeding increment. This time-bounded approach ensures that each module is properly developed and evaluated while maintaining steady progress in the overall system  development.

Each increment will focus on implementing specific modules and system functionalities, allowing the researchers to progressively build, evaluate, and refine the system until the complete platform is achieved.

Current solutions often rely on multiple specialized tools to address different operational needs, which can fragment workflows and reduce administrative oversight. These gaps highlight opportunities for a centralized platform that can unify key processes and improve clinic efficiency, data accessibility, and service quality.

Their findings indirectly reinforce the value of client-visible EMR ecosystems that enhance transparency and care coordination.

More recent literature further demonstrates the expanding role of EMR infrastructures. Davies et al. Moreover, they emphasized that EHR systems substantially expand pharmacovigilance capabilities when supported by appropriate text-mining and standardization methods.

In a related safety-focused investigation, Petrou et al. (2025) examined veterinary electronic health records as a mechanism for identifying medication errors in clinical practice. The authors found that EHR datasets can reveal dosing errors and other treatment risks that are often underreported in voluntary systems. Their analysis underscores the growing importance of EMR infrastructures for improving patient safety and clinical governance in veterinary settings.

From the client engagement perspective, According to Aristek Systems (2025), client portals integrated into veterinary EHR platforms allow pet owners to view vaccination records, appointment histories, and treatment information in real time. The article explained that this transparency strengthens trust, increases client participation, and improves adherence to veterinary recommendations, demonstrating the rising importance of customer-accessible EMR features in modern veterinary service delivery.

The study demonstrated that large, well-structured EMR datasets enable the development of advanced analytics and natural language processing tools for veterinary medicine. The authors emphasized that expanding access to standardized digital records can accelerate innovations in animal health monitoring and comparative biomedical research.

Results indicated that appropriate distribution of tasks improved clinic productivity while reducing the workload of veterinarians, which ultimately contributed to the financial sustainability of veterinary practices. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating operational strategies to ensure efficient use of resources in veterinary clinics. In the context of the present study, veterinary clinic systems can help track staff responsibilities, service activities, and operational expenditures, thereby providing valuable information for conducting cost-benefit analysis.
Synthesis

The reviewed literature demonstrates the increasing use of digital technologies in veterinary healthcare to improve clinic operations, service accessibility, and information management. Across the different studies, researchers consistently describe the movement from manual administrative processes toward computerized systems that support veterinary services, client interaction, and clinic management functions. These developments illustrate how digital systems contribute to more organized veterinary operations and improved service delivery.

Research on veterinary management systems shows that early system implementations were developed to address challenges associated with paper-based records and manual appointment scheduling. According to Jaffar and Zin (2021), web-based veterinary platforms were initially introduced to facilitate online registration, appointment scheduling, and access to treatment information, thereby improving service coordination. Later studies expanded these capabilities by enabling secure storage of medical histories, appointment monitoring, and generation of administrative reports that support clinic management (Jamil, 2023; Ahmad & Salamat, 2023). More recent research demonstrates that veterinary management systems now include additional modules such as inventory tracking, financial management, and centralized record sharing among clinics (Abd Latiff & Aziz, 2025; Guale Vera, 2025; Silva & Reis, 2025). These developments indicate that modern veterinary information systems increasingly support comprehensive operational management within clinical environments.

Studies examining online appointment scheduling in veterinary clinics show that digital booking systems improve accessibility and organization of veterinary services. Researchers report that web-based scheduling platforms reduce reliance on phone-based booking and allow pet owners to arrange consultations more conveniently (Blancaflor et al., 2023; Bucao et al., 2023). In addition, several investigations demonstrate that online scheduling contributes to reduced administrative workload and fewer booking errors (Rosmani & Mokhtar, 2023). Empirical findings further indicate measurable improvements in clinic operations, including decreased appointment no-show rates, increased appointment utilization, and improved after-hours booking accessibility (Cachuela et al., 2025; Larkin, 2023; MWI Animal Health, 2024). These results show that online scheduling systems play a significant role in improving veterinary service accessibility and appointment management.

The literature also discusses the growing use of online consultation and telemedicine in veterinary practice. Studies show that telehealth platforms improve access to veterinary care, particularly for clients who experience transportation or financial limitations (Lundahl et al., 2022; Naimark et al., 2022). Remote consultations allow veterinarians to provide guidance, follow-up care, and preliminary assessments without requiring immediate physical visits, which may reduce stress for animals and increase convenience for pet owners (Addae, 2023; Guintard et al., 2024). Despite these advantages, researchers note that adoption may be influenced by factors such as technological familiarity, regulatory policies, and concerns regarding diagnostic limitations in remote consultations (Abu-Seida, 2024; Springer, 2024). Nevertheless, recent studies indicate growing interest in hybrid care approaches that combine digital consultation with traditional in-clinic examinations (Neill, 2025; Karsch, 2026).

Another important component discussed in the literature is the implementation of electronic medical record (EMR) systems in veterinary clinics. These systems support efficient documentation, retrieval, and sharing of animal health information. According to Ouyang (2021), modern veterinary practice increasingly requires digital tools that allow effective communication and information exchange between veterinarians and pet owners. Subsequent studies confirm that EMR systems improve clinical documentation processes and facilitate continuity of care by allowing veterinarians to access patient histories more easily (Ahmed et al., 2023). Furthermore, electronic records provide valuable resources for broader veterinary research, disease surveillance, and medication monitoring when large numbers of records are examined collectively (Fins et al., 2023; Davies et al., 2024). Client portals connected to these systems also enable pet owners to review vaccination records, treatment histories, and appointment information, strengthening transparency and client participation in animal healthcare (Aristek Systems, 2025).

The reviewed studies also emphasize the importance of queue management systems in improving service flow within healthcare environments, including veterinary clinics. Research indicates that digital queue systems allow clinics to monitor waiting lines, organize service order, and reduce waiting time (Bidari et al., 2021; Ala et al., 2022). Implementations of electronic queue platforms have been shown to reduce congestion in reception areas and improve patient flow within clinical facilities (Okunade et al., 2024; Rachmawati et al., 2024). Additional investigations demonstrate that advanced queue optimization techniques, including predictive modeling and automated monitoring tools, can further improve service responsiveness and reduce waiting stress among clients (Tshiamala et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest that digital queue management contributes to more organized and efficient service processes in veterinary clinics.

In addition, several studies discuss the role of service performance reporting systems in supporting organizational monitoring and evaluation. Digital reporting frameworks allow institutions to record operational indicators and generate reports that support management decision-making (Tiron-Tudor et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024). Automated reporting tools also help reduce errors associated with manual documentation while improving transparency and accountability in service operations (Santos et al., 2024; OECD, 2025). Through structured performance monitoring, institutions can better assess service quality, identify operational issues, and support continuous improvement efforts.

Finally, the literature emphasizes the relevance of the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model in evaluating veterinary information systems. Studies show that this framework provides a structured approach for assessing software quality characteristics such as functionality, usability, reliability, security, performance efficiency, maintainability, and compatibility (Iskandar et al., 2023; Matias et al., 2025). Research further indicates that veterinary systems must ensure secure handling of clinical information, dependable system operation, and user-friendly interfaces to support effective veterinary service delivery (Bök et al., 2024; Ganiron et al., 2026). Applying ISO25010 therefore provides a comprehensive basis for evaluating the quality and effectiveness of veterinary clinic information systems.

Overall, the reviewed literature indicates that digital veterinary systems play a significant role in improving clinic management, service accessibility, and veterinary healthcare delivery. The studies collectively show that technologies such as online appointment scheduling, teleconsultation platforms, electronic medical records, queue management systems, and performance reporting tools help address limitations associated with manual clinic processes. At the same time, the literature suggests that successful system implementation depends on usability, technical infrastructure, and regulatory considerations. These insights provide a strong foundation for developing veterinary information systems that effectively support both clinic operations and client engagement.
Software Methodology

The researchers will use the Incremental Development Model for the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The researcher will use the model to allow developing the system by dividing the requirements in parts of functional modules called increments, where each increment adds new features and improvements to the system until the final product is completed. The proposed system incremental will first undergo requirement analysis, followed by design and development, testing, and deployment of each module. Each increment will produce a working portion of the system that will be evaluated and refined before proceeding to the next stage of development.

Figure 3 illustrates the Incremental Development Model used in the development of the proposed iPawcus Veterinary Management System. The Incremental Model is a software development approach that focuses on building the system gradually through a series of smaller development cycles called increments. Each increment follows a structured process consisting of requirement analysis, system design, development, testing, and deployment, allowing a portion of the system to be completed and evaluated before moving on to the next stage. In this model, the core functionalities of the system are developed first, followed by additional features that enhance the system in later increments. Each increment produces a functional component of the system that can be tested and improved before integrating it into the overall platform. This process ensures that errors are identified early and that system improvements can be implemented continuously throughout development.

Every increment will have a minimum duration of one month and a maximum duration of one month and two weeks, depending on the complexity of the features being implemented. During this period, the researchers will conduct requirement adjustment, system design, module development, and testing activities before proceeding to the succeeding increment. This time-bounded approach ensures that each module is properly developed and evaluated while maintaining steady progress in the overall system  development.

Each increment will focus on implementing specific modules and system functionalities, allowing the researchers to progressively build, evaluate, and refine the system until the complete platform is achieved.

5.An offline mode with automatic data synchronization should be added to the iPawcus system to support selected clinic functions during internet interruptions. The feature should initially allow authorized personnel to save draft consultation notes and provisional records of medical supply usage on approved clinic devices. These entries should remain marked as pending until the connection is restored and the central system validates them. The feature should include safeguards to prevent duplicate entries, check current stock quantities, and resolve conflicting updates during synchronization. This development would help personnel retain essential information during temporary connectivity problems.

6.It is recommended that iPawcus undergo regular evaluation and maintenance based on user feedback and actual clinic operations. Future improvements should prioritize identified workflow limitations, consistency of records across related modules, verification of access restrictions, and checking of report calculations against their source records. Report and chart generation should also be examined because one end-user rated its response time as “Not Acceptable.” Updates should be tested before deployment to verify that existing functions continue to operate as intended. This would help the clinic identify recurring concerns and maintain the system as operational requirements change.

7.The interface and operation of the iPawcus system should be further improved in response to the IT experts’ Interaction Capability mean of 3.20, interpreted as “Acceptable.” Particular attention should be given to service transaction and inventory functions, whose ease of operation also received a mean of 3.20 from end-users. The improvements should include clearer navigation, consistent labels, brief instructions, and a review of the steps required to complete common tasks. The revised functions should be tested with their intended users to determine whether the changes make the tasks easier to complete. This would address the area receiving the lowest technical assessment.
